title: Use Meaningful Incentives needs-meaningful-incentives/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin recounts writing a spontaneous note of appreciation to a student named Joanna, whose emotional reaction and years-long habit of keeping every note he ever gave her convinced him that stickers, stamps, and similar tangible rewards are far less meaningful incentives than personal, handwritten recognition. He pairs this with a story about his principal Judy, whose private handwritten notes of praise left in his mailbox meant more to him as a new teacher than any group appreciation event, reinforcing his point that genuine, personal gestures carry outsized motivational weight. From these experiences he distills a set of practical guidelines for writing effective notes to students: use distinctive but inexpensive stationery, always handwrite rather than print, describe something specific that exceeded ordinary expectations, keep the note private, stay authentic rather than offering empty praise, deliver it before students arrive, and avoid drawing attention to it afterward. He argues that the most powerful incentives are unconnected to any explicit 'if you do this, you'll get that' bargain, arriving instead as unexpected, genuine recognition. The piece positions personal notes as a simple, low-cost but high-impact addition to a broader system of classroom incentives.
points: A personal, handwritten note of praise had far more lasting emotional impact on a student than stickers, stamps, or other tangible classroom incentives.
Private, personal recognition from a supervisor (illustrated by principal Judy's handwritten notes) can be more motivating to teachers than public appreciation events.
Practical guidelines for effective notes include always handwriting them, keeping them private, being specific and authentic, and delivering them before students arrive.
The most influential incentives are those not tied to an explicit behavioral bargain -- they arrive unexpectedly rather than as a transactional reward.
Teachers are cautioned against over-explaining or drawing attention to a note after giving it, letting the gesture itself communicate the message.
quotes: Many years ago, on a whim, I wrote a short note to a student named Joanna to let her know how much I appreciated her leadership qualities. I wrote the note before school one day and left it folded over and taped to her desk.
She pulled out a pencil box to show me where she had kept every note I had ever given her. They were stacked from oldest to newest, and at the bottom of the stack was my first note to her.

I’ve since learned that stickers, stamps, and the like are mostly ineffective. They’re fun to give out and students like them, but I don’t believe they make much difference; they don’t have any real meaning attached to them.
As a new teacher, shaky on confidence, her notes meant the world to me. There was no earthly way I was going to let her down or prove her positive words wrong.
Always handwrite the note. A computer-printed note is cold and lacks heart.
The most influential incentives are those that aren’t connected to a particular behavior, as in “do this and you’ll get that.” The best incentives are those that arrive out of the blue.
None of us are immune to the wonderful feeling of receiving a handwritten letter or note from someone we admire.
